text:
Season Journey


  
    Weeks 1–5
    Injury Chaos Begins
    Top draft picks sidelined early. Thanks to the strong roster dominating FG%, REB, AST, and BLK categories, I reached rank 2 early.
  

  
    Weeks 6–18
    Multiple Injuries, Holding Position
    Roster never fully healthy for 18 straight weeks. Utilized strategic waiver wire moves on category-specific strengths of REB, AST, and low TOs to maintain standings at rank 9.
  

  
    Week 19 — Turning Point
    🔑 Player come back + KD + Raynaud Trade
    4 players come back from injury after All-star break, and acquired Kevin Durant and Maxime Raynaud at low cost thanks to season ending sale. Projection model flagged an immediate boost across 3PT, PTS, STL.
  

  
    Weeks 19–21
    Roster at Full Strength
    Jokić, Durant, and Paul George all healthy simultaneously for the first time. Weekly win probabilities climbed above 85%.
  

  
    Week 22 — The Tank
    🎲 Strategic Seed 8 Decision
    Identified that Jokić and Clingan had only 2 games in Week 23 due to NBA scheduling. Deliberately lost Week 21 to drop to Seed 8, avoiding a top-seed semi-final during the weakest week.
  

  
    Weeks 23–24
    🏆 Playoff Dominance
    Semi-finals won against a mid-seed opponent despite Jokić's limited games. Finals entered with full roster and 91.7% simulated win probability.

title: 🏆 Championship Run
text:
The Technical Stack

  
    🤖
    Yahoo API Automation
    Daily automated pulls of roster stats, injury flags, and matchup data
       via OAuth. Output pushed directly to Excel reports each morning.
  
  
    🎲
    Monte Carlo Simulation
    100,000 simulations per matchup using Poisson distributions per player
       per game. Generated category-level and overall win probabilities.
  
  
    📊
    Excel Matchup Board
    Auto-generated weekly Excel boards showing projected vs. actual stats,
       games remaining, injury status, and category breakdowns.
  
  
    🏥
    Injury Tracking
    ESPN injury feed integrated with roster data. Automated GTD/OUT flags
       with season-average fallbacks to keep projections realistic.
  
  
    ⚗️
    Last-30 Baseline Stats
    Rolling 30-day averages as projection baseline, with season-stat
       fallback for players returning from injury.
  
  
    🌲
    Games Remaining Model
    NBA schedule scraper estimated remaining games per team each week,
       driving volume-adjusted projections that raw averages miss.

title: 🏆 Championship Run
text:
The Strategic Tank
My two best players had a critical NBA scheduling problem in Week 23:

Nikola Jokić — elite across all 7 categories, but only 2 games in Week 23
Donovan Clingan — elite REB + BLK, but only 2 games in Week 23

This made Week 23 my weakest week of the playoffs regardless of seeding. The key question was: which opponent do I face in that weak week?


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 6.5))
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(2, 1, hspace=0.7)

xs = [0.3, 4.2, 8.1]
week_labels = ['Week 22\n(Quarter-finals)', 'Week 23\n(Semi-finals)', 'Week 24\n(Finals)']
BOX_W, BOX_H = 3.5, 0.8

def draw_row(ax, title, title_color, boxes):
    ax.set_xlim(0, 12.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.6)
    ax.axis('off')
    ax.text(0.2, 1.52, title, color=title_color,
            fontsize=10.5, fontweight='bold', va='top')

    for i, (label, sub, color) in enumerate(boxes):
        x = xs[i]
        rect = mpatches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (x, 0.45), BOX_W, BOX_H,
            boxstyle="round,pad=0.1",
            linewidth=1.3, edgecolor='#bbbbbb',
            facecolor=color
        )
        ax.add_patch(rect)
        ax.text(x + BOX_W/2,
                0.45 + BOX_H/2 + (0.1 if sub else 0),
                label, ha='center', va='center',
                color='white', fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
        if sub:
            ax.text(x + BOX_W/2,
                    0.45 + BOX_H/2 - 0.18,
                    sub, ha='center', va='center',
                    color='#eeeeee', fontsize=7.8)
        ax.text(x + BOX_W/2, 0.38, week_labels[i],
                ha='center', va='top',
                color='#666666', fontsize=7.5)
        if i < len(boxes) - 1:
            ax.annotate('',
                xy=(xs[i+1] - 0.05, 0.45 + BOX_H/2),
                xytext=(x + BOX_W + 0.05, 0.45 + BOX_H/2),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#888888', lw=1.5))

# PATH A: Seed 3-6
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
draw_row(ax1,
    title='PATH A — Seed 3 to 6  (rejected)',
    title_color='#c62828',
    boxes=[
        ('QF: vs Seed 7/8',    '✅ Jokić 4G — Win easily',       '#2e7d32'),
        ('SF: vs Seed 1 or 2', '❌ Jokić only 2G — Cannot win',  '#c62828'),
        ('Finals: if reached', '⚠️ Never gets here',             '#9e9e9e'),
    ]
)
ax1.text(12.3, 0.85, '~8%\nchamp\nprob',
         ha='right', va='center', fontsize=8.5,
         color='#c62828', fontweight='bold')

# PATH B: Seed 8
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
draw_row(ax2,
    title='PATH B — Seed 8  ✓ chosen',
    title_color='#2e7d32',
    boxes=[
        ('QF: vs Seed 1',      '⚠️ Jokić 4G — 50/50',           '#e65100'),
        ('SF: vs Seed 4 or 5', '✅ Jokić 2G — Still winnable',   '#1565c0'),
        ('Finals: Week 24',    '✅ Full roster — 91.7% win prob', '#1b5e20'),
    ]
)
ax2.text(12.3, 0.85, '~16%\nchamp\nprob',
         ha='right', va='center', fontsize=8.5,
         color='#2e7d32', fontweight='bold')

fig.suptitle(
    "The Tank Decision: Jokić's Week 23 Schedule Determined Everything",
    fontsize=11.5, fontweight='bold', y=1.01
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

text:
Key Takeaways






TipWhat Made the Difference




Baseline quality — Last-30-day stats with injury-aware fallbacks gave realistic projections, not season averages skewed by early-season performance.
Games remaining model — Knowing a player has 4 games vs 2 games this week often matters more than per-game averages alone.
Simulation over gut feel — Monte Carlo revealed 3PM/TO were already lost before the week started, so focus shifted to winning the other 5 categories.
The tank was counter-intuitive — Conventional wisdom says chase the highest seed. The scheduling data showed the opposite was optimal.

title: Codex NBA Fantasy — Agentic Matchup Analytics
text:
Why I built this
Weekly fantasy decisions — who to start, who to stream, who to drop — are usually made on vibes. This project replaces the vibes with a reproducible pipeline: pull the live league state from Yahoo, project the next ~7 days of head-to-head category math, and ship a single Excel workbook that tells me exactly where my matchup is fragile and which waiver pickups would actually move those categories.
It runs on demand or on a daily cron, and it’s been the backbone of my real fantasy season.

title: Codex NBA Fantasy — Agentic Matchup Analytics
text:
What it produces
Each run writes one Excel workbook with four sheets:
Matchup Board. Head-to-head category projections for me vs. my scheduled opponent across the nine standard Yahoo categories (FG%, FT%, 3PTM, PTS, REB, AST, ST, BLK, TO). Three time slices per category — Now (already locked in), Future (remaining games × projected per-game), and Total. Makes it explicit whether a lead is real or fragile.
Average Impact. Season-average impact per player, with a graceful fallback to prior-season averages when the current sample is too small (GP < 10). This avoids the classic “one good game makes a stretch waiver pickup look elite” trap.
Free Agents. Ranked waiver-wire candidates filtered by which categories I am actually losing in this matchup, scored by remaining games × per-game impact on those categories. Not generic rest-of-season rankings — pickups specifically tuned to flip the categories that matter this week.
Injury Tracking Lists. A persistent watchlist of injured / suspended / low-availability players, merged from Yahoo statuses, ESPN’s injury feed, and free-text player notes. Each row carries a return-rate score, expected return date, the keyword that triggered the pickup (“questionable”, “doubtful”, “G-League”, “minutes restriction”…), a recency bucket, and per-game category impact. The sheet is reloaded from the previous run on every refresh, so dropoffs and upgrades day-over-day are visible.

title: Codex NBA Fantasy — Agentic Matchup Analytics
text:
Design notes
Stats are computed, not scraped. All projections come from the Yahoo Fantasy API. ESPN is used only for injury context.
Time-aware projections. Splitting each category into Now / Future / Total was the most useful UX choice in the whole project. A 12–11 lead in 3PTM looks different when Now is 10–4 vs. when Now is 2–9 — and the board makes that obvious without me having to mentally subtract.
Sample-size guardrails. Per-game rates fall back to season averages or prior-season averages when fewer than two games exist in the rolling window. Prevents waiver candidates from looking artificially elite off a single hot night.
Injury intelligence as a first-class feature. The Injury Tracking sheet isn’t just an INJ tag — it scores each watched player on (1) keyword urgency parsed from Yahoo player notes, (2) ESPN’s published expected return date, (3) recency of the news, and (4) per-category fantasy impact. Names listed in MANUAL_TRACK_PLAYERS are pinned regardless of status.
Name normalization. Yahoo, ESPN, and the NBA schedule feed disagree on accents, suffixes, and punctuation. external_injuries.normalize_name makes the joins reliable.
Token hygiene. Secrets in .env, OAuth tokens in data/yahoo_tokens.json, both gitignored.

title: Reducing Rental Returns with Fit Prediction
text:
Business problem
For a fashion-rental platform, a garment that doesn’t fit is expensive twice. It triggers a return, with shipping and cleaning costs, and it produces an unhappy customer who may not rent again. If the platform can predict whether a specific item will fit a specific renter, it can put the best-fitting items at the top of each customer’s results and cut avoidable returns.

title: Reducing Rental Returns with Fit Prediction
text:
Data
The data is the public Rent the Runway review dataset: 192,544 reviews from 105,571 users on 5,850 items. Each review records whether the item ran small, large, or fit. I collapsed small and large into not fit, which leaves a 74% / 26% class imbalance. I handled the imbalance with balanced class weights rather than resampling.





Fit label distribution: most rentals fit, and the misses split almost evenly between too small and too large.







Fit rate barely varies by body type, so broad body categories alone can’t predict fit.







Per-user fit rates are strongly bimodal. Fit is highly personal, which is why user-level signal matters.

title: Reducing Rental Returns with Fit Prediction
text:
Approach
Three feature families feed one scikit-learn pipeline:


Body & item numerics height, weight, bust, size, age: parsed from raw strings, imputed, scaled


Categoricals user, item, category, occasion, body type: one-hot


Review text TF-IDF on 1–2-grams, 10K features


ColumnTransformer → Logistic regression class-balanced


Rank items per user by predicted fit probability


Leakage control. I split train/validation/test by user (70 / 10 / 20). Each renter’s reviews appear in exactly one partition, so the test score reflects performance on customers the model has never seen.

title: Dallas Trinity FC: Fan Growth, Retention & Propensity Models
text:
How the models work together
The BAS was the core deliverable. I paired it with predictive models so that each business question has a score behind it:


Brand Affinity Score (Fan+) · Connection Who is this fan today? Scores each fan’s connection to the club from ticket and merchandise behavior, used to prioritize loyalty-program outreach.


Segment change · Loyalty Where is the relationship heading? Probability that a fan upgrades or downgrades over the next four home games.


Ticket propensity · Engagement How likely are they to buy right now? Probability of buying at least one ticket for the next four home games.


Growth & retention · Engagement & loyalty How many games will they attend? Expected attendance compared with the fan’s own recent baseline.

title: Dallas Trinity FC: Fan Growth, Retention & Propensity Models
text:
Pipeline


Fan data core: tickets & merchandise (2 seasons); enrichment: email, YouTube, TV, schedule


Feature engineering time-aligned to a snapshot date to prevent leakage


Rolling time-based CV train on past windows, test on the next


Models XGBoost vs. logistic and heuristic baselines


Explainability SHAP and permutation importance


CRM master file scores → action segments


Validating honestly. Fan behavior is seasonal and the data spans two seasons, so a random split would leak future information into training. I validated with rolling-origin folds instead: each model trains on earlier home-game windows and is tested on the next window. For the segment-change model, XGBoost beat both a rules-based heuristic and regularized logistic regression on AUC in every fold.

title: Dallas Trinity FC: Fan Growth, Retention & Propensity Models
text:
From scores to action
A model only creates value if the marketing team can use it. I translated the probability scores into plain-language segments, such as Upgrade Candidate, Retention Watchlist, and Stable / Low-Touch, and wrote them into a single CRM master file. The handoff package included:

an Analytical Guide that explains each model, its intended use, and its limits in non-technical language
a navigation guide to the deliverables and model-specific methodology notes
a reproducible refresh script, so the club can re-score fans each season without the project team
an executive presentation to the club’s senior marketing and data-strategy leadership

title: Dallas Trinity FC: Fan Growth, Retention & Propensity Models
text:
Lessons

Handoff design is part of the model. Documentation, segment labels, and a refresh path mattered as much as AUC.
Explainability builds trust. SHAP and permutation importance let non-technical stakeholders see why a fan was flagged.
Time alignment is the hardest part. Joining six sources with different grains and horizons required explicit snapshot logic to avoid leakage.

title: LINE Official Account: Lifecycle-Driven Pricing Strategy
text:
Business context
LINE Official Account is a subscription product that lets businesses message their customers on LINE. Revenue depends on moving accounts through a lifecycle: from free adoption, to a first paid plan, to higher tiers as usage grows.
Headquarters planned a pricing change to improve monetization. Most accounts were small and medium businesses, which are more price-sensitive and slower to mature. A uniform price increase risked raising short-term revenue while slowing conversion and long-term growth.

title: LINE Official Account: Lifecycle-Driven Pricing Strategy
text:
My role

Owned the analytical strategy end to end, partnering with Product, Sales, and Finance
Built the behavioral segmentation and lifecycle funnel analysis
Developed the pricing scenario framework and presented recommendations to leadership
Supported go-to-market rollout with dashboards for Sales and Product

title: LINE Official Account: Lifecycle-Driven Pricing Strategy
text:
Analytical approach
Instead of asking “how much should we charge?”, I asked “where in the lifecycle are customers getting stuck, and how does pricing cause it?”


Behavioral data usage, upgrades, account maturity


Lifecycle segmentation group accounts by stage and behavior


Funnel diagnosis measure friction between stages


Scenario modeling short- vs. long-term trade-offs


Recommendation to leadership


KPI monitoring dashboards for Sales and Product

title: LINE Official Account: Lifecycle-Driven Pricing Strategy
text:
Visual explanation
Where the lifecycle stalled. The funnel analysis found two main friction points. The segmentation showed that different customer groups hit them in different ways.


Acquisition


Activation


Free usage


First paid plan ⚠ conversion friction


Expansion ⚠ expansion friction


Retention



Conversion friction: many engaged accounts had little reason to move from free to paid, which delayed monetization.
Expansion friction: accounts whose usage kept growing still hesitated to move up a tier.

The recommendation rebalanced the free-to-paid and tier-to-tier transitions, so pricing encourages customers to progress instead of blocking them.
Why scenario modeling mattered. The scenario with the highest short-term revenue was not the best long-term strategy. The framework compared pricing options across the whole lifecycle, not just on immediate revenue.

title: Ipsos: Pricing & Brand Research Methods
section: Method demo: pricing a new subscription
text:
Method demo: pricing a new subscription
Illustrative demonstration using synthetic data. No client data is shown.
To show how I approach this kind of problem without reproducing any client work, this demo follows one fictional product: Brewly, a monthly coffee-bean subscription preparing to launch.

1. The research question

How should Brewly set an acceptable price range, understand the trade-offs customers will make, and check that its positioning works?

No single method answers all three parts, so each method is matched to one part:


Van Westendorp price sensitivity What price range will customers accept?


Conjoint analysis What will customers trade off: features, brand, service, or price?


Regression What drives purchase intent and brand perception?


Experiments Which message or concept performs better?




2. Van Westendorp: finding the acceptable price range
Respondents answer four questions. At what price would the product be too cheap to trust, cheap / a good deal, getting expensive, and too expensive to consider? Plotting the four cumulative curves shows where price resistance begins.



Synthetic Van Westendorp price sensitivity meter for the fictional Brewly subscription.


Illustrative demonstration using synthetic data. No client data is shown.
How to read it

Acceptable range (shaded): between the lower bound, where “too cheap” meets “expensive”, and the upper bound, where “cheap” meets “too expensive”. Pricing outside this band risks either a quality signal problem or outright rejection.
Candidate reference price: the optimal and indifference price points sit close together near the middle of the band. That gives a defensible anchor for the launch price.
Limitation: Van Westendorp tells you what customers find acceptable, not what they will choose against alternatives. That is why the next step matters.



3. Conjoint: understanding the trade-offs
A choice-based conjoint shows customers realistic packages side by side. Their choices reveal how much each feature is worth relative to price.



Synthetic relative attribute importance from a conjoint study.





Synthetic part-worth utilities for each attribute level.


Illustrative demonstration using synthetic data. No client data is shown.
From preferences to package design


Customer preferences part-worths by attribute


Trade-offs e.g., flexible pause/skip offsets part of a price step


Package design Basic / Core / Premium


Pricing & positioning lead with the Core package


In this synthetic example, a simulated market with three packages gives the mid-priced Core package (3 bags, flexible schedule) about half of the preference share. Most of its advantage comes from service flexibility rather than a lower price, which supports a positioning built on convenience, not discount.


4. Regression & experimentation
The two methods above set price and package. These two check why customers respond and what message to launch with.


Regression: drivers
Model purchase intent or brand perception on attribute ratings, such as taste, convenience, and value for money. The goal is to find which perceptions actually move the outcome, so the brand invests in the right claims.


Experiments: concept & message tests
Randomly show matched groups different concepts, ads, or positioning statements. Compare purchase intent and choice, then roll out the winner with measurable confidence.




5. The decision framework


Customer research


Price sensitivity + Feature trade-offs + Brand / positioning response Van Westendorp · conjoint · regression · experiments


Commercial recommendation price range, package line-up, launch message


The point of the research is not any single chart. It is one recommendation that pricing, product, and marketing teams can all act on.
Brewly is fictional and every value on this page is synthetic. The demo shows methodology only and does not represent any Ipsos client engagement.

title: KPMG: SROI & Investment Decision Modeling
section: Method demo: from sustainability project to investment decision
text:
Method demo: from sustainability project to investment decision
Illustrative demonstration using synthetic data. Client financial information and project assumptions are not shown.

1. What SROI measures
SROI asks a business question about a social or environmental program: for every dollar invested, how much value does it create? Answering it means tracing the chain from spending to outcomes, then putting a monetary value on those outcomes.


Investment program budget


Activities what the program does


Outputs people reached, sessions held


Stakeholder outcomes what changes for them


Monetized benefits financial proxies, adjusted for attribution


SROI → decision




SROI = value created ÷ investment An SROI of 3.0 means each $1 invested creates about $3 of social and economic value.




2. Cost-benefit analysis: finding where value is created
A single program-level SROI hides a lot. Breaking the program into components shows which activities create the most value per dollar, and which ones drain the budget.



Synthetic value-per-dollar by component for a fictional environmental-education program.


Illustrative demonstration using synthetic data. Client financial information and project assumptions are not shown.


Current design one blended SROI


Component view value per $ by activity


Find high-cost / low-impact e.g., printed materials above


Reallocate or reprice shift budget to high-value activities


More value per $


In the real engagement, this kind of analysis led to pricing and program-design recommendations that raised average SROI by about 10%. The chart above is fictional and does not reproduce that client’s figures.


3. Smart-city investment case: which areas are worth expanding into?
The second example is a P&L forecast for a fictional smart-streetlight rollout, comparing three deployment scenarios.


Upfront investment


Operating & maintenance cost


Revenue & economic benefit


Deployment scenario urban / suburban / rural


P&L forecast


Expansion decision





Synthetic comparison: a first-look revenue metric vs. a full P&L view across three deployment scenarios.


Illustrative demonstration using synthetic data. Client financial information and project assumptions are not shown.
The insight: judged on a headline metric, the rural scenario looks least attractive. Once upfront cost, operating cost, and benefits are modeled over the asset’s life, the ranking can change. A segment that is easy to dismiss can turn out to be an economically viable expansion opportunity. That was the kind of conclusion the real forecast supported.

Why this matters to the rest of my work. KPMG is where I started turning qualitative “should we do this?” questions into quantified investment cases. That habit carried through customer and pricing research at Ipsos and into product and pricing decisions at LINE.
Both projects on this page are fictional and every value is synthetic. The demo shows methodology only and does not represent any KPMG client engagement.

title: Redesigning a Promotional Ad Package with Segment & Timing Analysis
text:
Business context
To drive revenue during a period of low market demand, the product team launched a limited-time promotional ad package with bundles tailored to different client groups. On paper the design was careful and incorporated sales feedback, but after launch it significantly underperformed, and senior management started to worry.
The package belonged to another team. My routine KPI tracking across sales channels showed me the performance gap, and I volunteered to investigate.

title: Redesigning a Promotional Ad Package with Segment & Timing Analysis
text:
My role

Identified the problem and took on the analysis without a formal mandate
Analyzed sales results across hundreds of clients and several sales channels (Excel, Tableau)
Diagnosed the structural causes and proposed a revised offer and launch timing
Partnered with the product manager to refine the plan and win buy-in, presenting it as iteration rather than critique

title: Redesigning a Promotional Ad Package with Segment & Timing Analysis
text:
Analytical approach
The team’s first hypothesis was simply “demand is low.” I wanted to know whether the design of the offer was part of the problem.


Low adoption symptom


Segment analysis who is (and isn’t) buying?


Offer analysis does the offer fit each segment?


Timing analysis does launch timing match buying cycles?


Root-cause diagnosis


Redesign


Rollout with the PM

title: Redesigning a Promotional Ad Package with Segment & Timing Analysis
text:
Visual explanation
Three lenses on one problem. No single view explained the underperformance. The answer came from looking at customer segments, offer structure, and timing together:


Customer segment Client groups differ in buying power and buying behavior. Who is the offer actually reaching?


Offer structure The incentive has to be relevant to each group. Is the value concentrated where it drives the most incremental purchases?


Timing Buying cycles differ by group. Does the launch window match when each group plans and spends?


Diagnosis The analysis found two structural design flaws: one in how the offer was distributed across client groups, and one in how launch timing lined up with their buying cycles.


The redesign tailored the offer and its timing to each client group, based on that group’s buying power and past seasonal behavior.

  Package sales (indexed to the original launch = 1×)
  Original package1×
  Redesigned package~20×

The redesigned package delivered about 20× the sales of the original launch
The analysis was later expanded into a standing framework for clients’ annual deals, used to assess each client’s true spending power rather than relying on past order size alone
It showed how cross-channel KPI tracking can reveal structural issues that are hard to see from inside a single team
